SA Crime Statistics 2018

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Crime statistics for 2018 have been released and paint a disquieting picture for South Africans' sense of safety. But could they be used to improve the way we fight crime?

Unique Selling Point:
Even though the latest crime statistics are shocking and some of the highest we've seen in South Africa, can they help in the way we fight crime?

Summary:
Not only do the latest crime statistics paint a distressing picture for South Africans' security, but for some communities the murder rates even rival those of war torn countries. Limpopo on the other hand is the province with the lowest murder rate, only 15 per 100 000, as compared to the overall figure of 35.8 per 100 000 people murdered.

From even these broad observations it is clear that the crime statistics can help target attention on certain communities. In other words the latest crime statistics are shocking and some of the highest we've seen in South Africa, but they could help in the way we fight crime says Dr Chris de Kock. However, the biggest problem especially when it comes to murder, aggravated robbery and rape, is there aren't enough sub categories within the statistics to formulate effective strategies for crime fighting and crime prevention. Even so the South African Police could be utilising the data more effectively.

For example 2.6 percent of the country's police stations recorded 21% of the murders throughout the country, 13% of police stations recorded 50% of all murders, if the police were to target resources on these specific precincts with more vigour, they might be able to bring the overall crime rate down by a significant amount.

What factors have driven up the numbers in serious crimes? Minister of Police Bheki Cele says, the police have dropped the ball. Carte Blanche takes a harder look at what it would really take to change the country's overall safety.

Further information:
Minister of Police Bheki Cele says, the only way to fight the current rise in crime is to utilise resources more effectively and to show criminals that there will be no tolerance. This he did as Police commissioner in 2009 to 2012. Visibility is the key. He says, the overall police morale is low and this has to be rectified. He wants police stations to be places of safety and trust for people and communities. Currently there is no faith in the police by ordinary citizens.

Dr Chris de Kock, who was with SAPS for 19 years working on crime statistics, is releasing a paper next week as to why the way the statistics are broken down and released are not assisting in crime prevention overall. For example, Booysens had the highest carjacking rate in South Africa, and statistically it has decreased but the only reason is, that the area was divided in two, now including Moffatville which brings the carjacking rate down, but if you had to add the two together they would be even higher than before. This situation has been ongoing for at least 9 years, one begs the question why would police not target that particular crime in that area and use the intelligence that statistics provide to combat this crime? This type of situation goes for other types of crimes too. Khayelitsha for example has the second highest murder rate in the country, but when you look at the statistics they are not broken down as to the types of murder, eg domestic, gang related and vigilante, which would clearly help the police in the way they approach reducing these types of crimes with regards to the strategies employed. Also in this area 65% of the murders occur at night and on weekends, this means that policing should be targeted during that time frame. Other examples that we will explore is street robbery which is 57% of aggravated robbery but is not broken down by the police and these are the criminals who ultimately gravitate to more serious crimes, as they are not deterred when they enter crime.

Gareth Newham from the ISS, will expand on why crime and violence are interrelated in our society . He says the figures for the way crime is combated are skewed. We spend 132B rand on criminal justice and only 9B rand on crime prevention. Most of what the SA government does is reactionary rather than looking at intervention packages like Inspire, from WHO, which has been used to bring down crime in many countries.

He also brings home that even though the rape statistics and sexual assault rate is up, it means that it is even bleaker in reality, because if reporting goes up, we know that under reporting also goes up.

We also set straight and look at farm murders within the overall murder rate and why it isn't as dire as some might want us to think, although they do have consequences in terms of losing skilled farmers who form part of food security in South Africa.

Chandre Gould from the ISS, addresses why South Africa as a country is so violent. We have 4 cities listed in the top 50 most violent cities in the world, and Cape Town is at number 11. One third of children have experienced violence in the home and at school. One of the biggest problems is the residue of violence and fatherless households. She states that the only way to change is the crime rate going forward is to change the societal issues that are creating fertile ground for future violence.

Overall, When we look at unemployment, even though Zimbabwe has a much higher unemployment rate than South Africa, we have far more crime, and this is because we have such extreme inequality.

Police Commissioner, General Khehla Sithole, needs to answer the burning questions, especially after the minister has undertaken to change the current crime wave. What is going to be done, and what kind of strategies are going to be implemented to affect change in crime?
The treatment will be to use Carte Blanche stories that cover the major categories of crime that we will be dealing with as visual material. Using the presenter to take us and do dynamic links in quite live situations eg Booysens for carjacking and Honeydew for house robbery. He will also do links using the interactive map to take us to places where we can't go physically, eg Phillippi and Stellenbosch for example. Well laid out and structured graphics will create the visual thread through the statistics.

Press Release:


Every year we get crime statistics, that provide information. The question is how are police using this intelligence to strategise against crime?

Script:


VO: Each day South Africa records, 110 rapes, 428 common assaults, 458 assaults with intent to do grievous bodily harm, 625 house burglaries and 45 car hijackings, these are some of the shocking crime statistics released for the year 2017/2018, but where do we begin to put all this right ?//

VO: Recently appointed Minister of Police Bheki Cele, laid down the law.

Cele: Work on high profile crimes like cash heist, attack of the malls, people getting robbed inside their houses and that kind of thing. Sharpen the units, sharpen the morale, you put the resources people will work

LINK: Although our crime rate is very high, we cannot compare it on a national level to war torn areas. But several precincts in South Africa have a murder rate that exceed the top 5 conflict zones in the world with a murder rate of over 100 people per hundred thousand. // For example in Philippi.

VO: Philippi East, a township of Cape Town has an estimated 323.4 murders per 100 000 people, higher than that of Syria with 212 murders per 100 000 .

Cele: We shall not allow criminals to go amok threatening the SA innocent citizens whoever wants to take us toe to toe we will come toe to toe

VO: A tough stance from the Minister - but intelligence, derived from DATA, is a key component for steering crime fighting priorities. A targeted interpretation of the statistics will enable the police to do a better job//


Dr Chris de Kock worked for the South African police in crime statistics analysis for 19 years. //

Chris: If you go to Britain, if you go to the United States, if you go to many of these countries you will find that your crime stats is the basis of policing, we talk about intelligence policing it is your registration of crime, the information that is on the docket. At station level you must know the where, the when, the what, what crimes, specifically the sub-category and who of that crime.

VO: Dr de Kock is critical of the way South Africa releases its crime statistics and says they are not broken down into enough targeted categories. This makes it difficult to strategise the correct approach in decreasing a particular crime.

Chris: For different kinds of murder you need different strategies, when you look at vigilantism, is there association, is there a group of people, or is it just spontaneous but that only your intelligence gatherers can tell you.

VO: Gareth Newham heads the Justice & Violence Prevention Programme, for the Institute for Security Studies (ISS). He asserts the police do have the information but are not releasing it for the use of other role players.

Gareth: The way the crime stats are released do not help crime prevention in any way. They are out of date when they are released, secondly the categories are broad so they look at total contact crime which range from murders, robberies, rape. In a single category like murder there is not one reason why people get murdered.

LINK: South Africa ranks in the top 20 most dangerous countries in the world to live in. With 56 murders happening every day. So what do these statistics tell us about who we are as a country?

Chandre: What it tells us is violence is very high in our society, Violence has become a normal way of being in SA.

VO: Dr Chandré Gould is a Senior Research Fellow, on the Justice & Violence Prevention Programme, for the Institute for Security Studies (ISS). Over the years her research has led her to believe that a further breakdown of the statistics is an imperative, for example the murder of women and children.

Chandre: Not only knowing so many murders were murders of women and so many were murders of children but also what age group of children

VO: 2930 murders of women and children were recorded during the 2017/2018 period, but the breakdown into specific categories, is not easily accessible by the police and requires deep analysis which is time consuming. Different strategies are needed to combat different crime types within this category, like femicide, robbery or even gang related violence

Chandre: Further disaggregated statistics could be useful in determining in where we put our resources but then someone has to use those statistics

VO: Police Commissioner, General Khehla Sithole may be new in his appointment but has years of policing experience and says strategies to increase analysis of crimes are being implemented

General: In the recent crime stats we have received few requests to expand, so we are able to give more information. I think we expanded on the crimes that affects farms.

VO: South African farm murders have been touted as genocide in some parts of the world, but a total of 62 farm murders, is not out of line with murder trends in the national crime statistics. So why has this sub-category been singled out for attention?

Gareth: We know that farm unions are very wealthy, very organised and they are able to utilize their resources to make sure this issue gets attention whereas poor people living in Nyanga don’t have the same levels of resources.

Chris: You know the moment you you start arguments for or against release of selective small categories of murders, you go into a dilemma and why I am for full disclosure of all the categories of murders.

VO: To address crime head-on Commissioner Sithole is re-establishing and introducing specialised units, to combat specific crimes like taxi violence and gangsterism. His priority is murder.

General: In October i’m reviving murder and robbery unit to respond to murders within a short space of time

VO: Some of these specialised units will be mobilised nearest to where they are needed most.

General: Each geographical approach area warrants its own specific intervention, we've got the gangs in the Western Cape there we executing the gang combat and prevention strategy.

Chris: If statistics were used in an intelligent way, If you go to phillipe east and do analysis, you will find that gang related murders are specifically high, it differs from Khayelitsha which is next door, in Khayelitsha it’s robbery, street robbery, the reaction is vigilantism, and then you have domestic and so on.. So you have to have high visibility, based on your patterns of crime.

Gareth: So they should be saying, let’s look at murder in different precincts where we have high murder rates, identify using information intelligence to see éxactly what factors are causing murders and then target our resources.

Chandre: We know that the poorer you are the more likely you are to experience crime and we know that of those people who are murdered the majority are young black men.

LINK: South Africans are constantly living in fear, house break ins, and robberies are a daily occurrence. Honeydew in Gauteng has been number one in terms of house robberies for a couple of years.

General: Honeydew is a city within another city but they are policed by 1 station the population grew and the station resources could not grow.

VO: The police are hoping that a new 24 hour Modus Operandi Centre, will halt crimes before they begin.

General: You can follow one crime and kill it, but the modus operandi can generate a million - of the same crime.

LINK: 57% of all robberies occur on the street, putting the most vulnerable people in our society at risk, those who walk and use public transport to get to places. But the significance of street robbery has far reaching consequences.

Gareth: One of the big challenges with police are not taking street robberies seriously enough, they don’t have anti robbery teams in high robbery areas.

Chris: You see how these people start off with street robbery and then they go to richer areas for house robbery, when they get a firearm and then they go for more organized crime like car jacking and later they become cash in transit robbers.

Gareth: Because if you hit street robberies hard over time the next decade you see reduction in all forms of robbery.

VO: However, it will take more than just policing to resolve the systemic and violent nature of crime in South Africa.

Chandre: If we don’t address poverty and inequality we are not going to get high levels of violence down. Violence and poverty and inequality have a reciprocal relationship.


Cele: One thing I’ll put my head on the block things will change.

Chandre: The police are one component in a far bigger system that needs to address violence, if we want to see violence come down, we all have a responsibility.

A targeted interpretation of the statistics will enable the police to do a better job// Dr Chris de Kock worked for the South African police in crime statistics analysis for 19 years. // Chris: If you go to Britain, if you go to the United States, if you go to many of these countries you will find that your crime stats is the basis of policing, we talk about intelligence policing it is your registration of crime, the information that is on the docket. At station level you must know the where, the when, the what, what crimes, specifically the sub-category and who of that crime. VO: Dr de Kock is critical of the way South Africa releases its crime statistics and says they are not broken down into enough targeted categories. This makes it difficult to strategise the correct approach in decreasing a particular crime. Chris: For different kinds of murder you need different strategies, when you look at vigilantism, is there association, is there a group of people, or is it just spontaneous but that only your intelligence gatherers can tell you. VO: Gareth Newham heads the Justice & Violence Prevention Programme, for the Institute for Security Studies (ISS). He asserts the police do have the information but are not releasing it for the use of other role players. Gareth: The way the crime stats are released do not help crime prevention in any way. They are out of date when they are released, secondly the categories are broad so they look at total contact crime which range from murders, robberies, rape. In a single category like murder there is not one reason why people get murdered. LINK: South Africa ranks in the top 20 most dangerous countries in the world to live in. With 56 murders happening every day. So what do these statistics tell us about who we are as a country? Chandre: What it tells us is violence is very high in our society, Violence has become a normal way of being in SA. VO: Dr Chandré Gould is a Senior Research Fellow, on the Justice & Violence Prevention Programme, for the Institute for Security Studies (ISS). Over the years her research has led her to believe that a further breakdown of the statistics is an imperative, for example the murder of women and children. Chandre: Not only knowing so many murders were murders of women and so many were murders of children but also what age group of children VO: 2930 murders of women and children were recorded during the 2017/2018 period, but the breakdown into specific categories, is not easily accessible by the police and requires deep analysis which is time consuming. Different strategies are needed to combat different crime types within this category, like femicide, robbery or even gang related violence Chandre: Further disaggregated statistics could be useful in determining in where we put our resources but then someone has to use those statistics VO: Police Commissioner, General Khehla Sithole may be new in his appointment but has years of policing experience and says strategies to increase analysis of crimes are being implemented General: In the recent crime stats we have received few requests to expand, so we are able to give more information. I think we expanded on the crimes that affects farms. VO: South African farm murders have been touted as genocide in some parts of the world, but a total of 62 farm murders, is not out of line with murder trends in the national crime statistics. So why has this sub-category been singled out for attention? Gareth: We know that farm unions are very wealthy, very organised and they are able to utilize their resources to make sure this issue gets attention whereas poor people living in Nyanga don’t have the same levels of resources. Chris: You know the moment you you start arguments for or against release of selective small categories of murders, you go into a dilemma and why I am for full disclosure of all the categories of murders. VO: To address crime head-on Commissioner Sithole is re-establishing and introducing specialised units, to combat specific crimes like taxi violence and gangsterism. His priority is murder. General: In October i’m reviving murder and robbery unit to respond to murders within a short space of time VO: Some of these specialised units will be mobilised nearest to where they are needed most. General: Each geographical approach area warrants its own specific intervention, we've got the gangs in the Western Cape there we executing the gang combat and prevention strategy. Chris: If statistics were used in an intelligent way, If you go to phillipe east and do analysis, you will find that gang related murders are specifically high, it differs from Khayelitsha which is next door, in Khayelitsha it’s robbery, street robbery, the reaction is vigilantism, and then you have domestic and so on.. So you have to have high visibility, based on your patterns of crime. Gareth: So they should be saying, let’s look at murder in different precincts where we have high murder rates, identify using information intelligence to see éxactly what factors are causing murders and then target our resources. Chandre: We know that the poorer you are the more likely you are to experience crime and we know that of those people who are murdered the majority are young black men. LINK: South Africans are constantly living in fear, house break ins, and robberies are a daily occurrence. Honeydew in Gauteng has been number one in terms of house robberies for a couple of years. General: Honeydew is a city within another city but they are policed by 1 station the population grew and the station resources could not grow. VO: The police are hoping that a new 24 hour Modus Operandi Centre, will halt crimes before they begin. General: You can follow one crime and kill it, but the modus operandi can generate a million - of the same crime. LINK: 57% of all robberies occur on the street, putting the most vulnerable people in our society at risk, those who walk and use public transport to get to places. But the significance of street robbery has far reaching consequences. Gareth: One of the big challenges with police are not taking street robberies seriously enough, they don’t have anti robbery teams in high robbery areas. Chris: You see how these people start off with street robbery and then they go to richer areas for house robbery, when they get a firearm and then they go for more organized crime like car jacking and later they become cash in transit robbers. Gareth: Because if you hit street robberies hard over time the next decade you see reduction in all forms of robbery. VO: However, it will take more than just policing to resolve the systemic and violent nature of crime in South Africa. Chandre: If we don’t address poverty and inequality we are not going to get high levels of violence down. Violence and poverty and inequality have a reciprocal relationship. Cele: One thing I’ll put my head on the block things will change. Chandre: The police are one component in a far bigger system that needs to address violence, if we want to see violence come down, we all have a responsibility.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Crime statistics for 2018 have been released and paint a disquieting picture for South Africans' sense of safety. But could they be used to improve the way we fight crime?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Even though the latest crime statistics are shocking and some of the highest we've seen in South Africa, can they help in the way we fight crime?
metadata.Summary: Not only do the latest crime statistics paint a distressing picture for South Africans' security, but for some communities the murder rates even rival those of war torn countries. Limpopo on the other hand is the province with the lowest murder rate, only 15 per 100 000, as compared to the overall figure of 35.8 per 100 000 people murdered. From even these broad observations it is clear that the crime statistics can help target attention on certain communities. In other words the latest crime statistics are shocking and some of the highest we've seen in South Africa, but they could help in the way we fight crime says Dr Chris de Kock. However, the biggest problem especially when it comes to murder, aggravated robbery and rape, is there aren't enough sub categories within the statistics to formulate effective strategies for crime fighting and crime prevention. Even so the South African Police could be utilising the data more effectively. For example 2.6 percent of the country's police stations recorded 21% of the murders throughout the country, 13% of police stations recorded 50% of all murders, if the police were to target resources on these specific precincts with more vigour, they might be able to bring the overall crime rate down by a significant amount. What factors have driven up the numbers in serious crimes? Minister of Police Bheki Cele says, the police have dropped the ball. Carte Blanche takes a harder look at what it would really take to change the country's overall safety.
metadata.Further information: Minister of Police Bheki Cele says, the only way to fight the current rise in crime is to utilise resources more effectively and to show criminals that there will be no tolerance. This he did as Police commissioner in 2009 to 2012. Visibility is the key. He says, the overall police morale is low and this has to be rectified. He wants police stations to be places of safety and trust for people and communities. Currently there is no faith in the police by ordinary citizens. Dr Chris de Kock, who was with SAPS for 19 years working on crime statistics, is releasing a paper next week as to why the way the statistics are broken down and released are not assisting in crime prevention overall. For example, Booysens had the highest carjacking rate in South Africa, and statistically it has decreased but the only reason is, that the area was divided in two, now including Moffatville which brings the carjacking rate down, but if you had to add the two together they would be even higher than before. This situation has been ongoing for at least 9 years, one begs the question why would police not target that particular crime in that area and use the intelligence that statistics provide to combat this crime? This type of situation goes for other types of crimes too. Khayelitsha for example has the second highest murder rate in the country, but when you look at the statistics they are not broken down as to the types of murder, eg domestic, gang related and vigilante, which would clearly help the police in the way they approach reducing these types of crimes with regards to the strategies employed. Also in this area 65% of the murders occur at night and on weekends, this means that policing should be targeted during that time frame. Other examples that we will explore is street robbery which is 57% of aggravated robbery but is not broken down by the police and these are the criminals who ultimately gravitate to more serious crimes, as they are not deterred when they enter crime. Gareth Newham from the ISS, will expand on why crime and violence are interrelated in our society . He says the figures for the way crime is combated are skewed. We spend 132B rand on criminal justice and only 9B rand on crime prevention. Most of what the SA government does is reactionary rather than looking at intervention packages like Inspire, from WHO, which has been used to bring down crime in many countries. He also brings home that even though the rape statistics and sexual assault rate is up, it means that it is even bleaker in reality, because if reporting goes up, we know that under reporting also goes up. We also set straight and look at farm murders within the overall murder rate and why it isn't as dire as some might want us to think, although they do have consequences in terms of losing skilled farmers who form part of food security in South Africa. Chandre Gould from the ISS, addresses why South Africa as a country is so violent. We have 4 cities listed in the top 50 most violent cities in the world, and Cape Town is at number 11. One third of children have experienced violence in the home and at school. One of the biggest problems is the residue of violence and fatherless households. She states that the only way to change is the crime rate going forward is to change the societal issues that are creating fertile ground for future violence. Overall, When we look at unemployment, even though Zimbabwe has a much higher unemployment rate than South Africa, we have far more crime, and this is because we have such extreme inequality. Police Commissioner, General Khehla Sithole, needs to answer the burning questions, especially after the minister has undertaken to change the current crime wave. What is going to be done, and what kind of strategies are going to be implemented to affect change in crime? The treatment will be to use Carte Blanche stories that cover the major categories of crime that we will be dealing with as visual material. Using the presenter to take us and do dynamic links in quite live situations eg Booysens for carjacking and Honeydew for house robbery. He will also do links using the interactive map to take us to places where we can't go physically, eg Phillippi and Stellenbosch for example. Well laid out and structured graphics will create the visual thread through the statistics.
